text:
Standard SASRec learns from item IDs and interaction order; titles are absent from its input ([original implementation](https://github.com/kang205/SASRec)). Consequently, editing titles while keeping IDs fixed cannot affect an ID-only model’s predictions. This implies that direct lexical dependence is unidentifiable through title edits; correlations between title similarity and recommendation scores can reflect shared behavioral structure. Substituting a different item ID changes its learned representation and interaction associations, confounding lexical and behavioral effects. Proposed controlled substitutions should independently vary title similarity and training-only behavioral similarity, matching popularity and history position; results establish associations or sensitivity to item identity, not causal use of words.

Cheaper controls target identifiable behavioral mechanisms: compare popularity, a smoothed last-item transition baseline, and recency-weighted item-to-item scores; then permute earlier history items while preserving the last item, history membership, padding and candidate set. This measures sensitivity to prefix order conditional on the latest interaction; truncating to the last item separately probes older-context contribution. These are proposed diagnostics, and inference-time permutations can introduce distribution shift. Supporting evidence: [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) report that simple recency-weighted pairwise probes outperform their eSASRec reproduction by 15–38% on three Amazon datasets under their protocol. Those gains do not transfer automatically to RecHarness’s pinned sampled-candidate evaluation. Run controls on unchanged validation splits and report macro HR@10 plus per-category results; low sensitivity supports limited dependence on the perturbed information, without proving the absence of higher-order learning.
